Curbside Pickup

The Home Depot · Curbside Pickup

The wait was short. The uncertainty was not.

Customers parked and waited without knowing whether the store knew they were there. I won support for a pilot that made arrival timing accessible through pickup emails and added check-in feedback to the app.

Role
Staff UX Designer
Scope
Field research, pilot proposal, pickup email, and app notifications
Key decision
Pair accessible arrival timing with feedback from the store
Outcome
A 50-store, 60-day pilot reported clearer expectations and fewer calls to switch fulfillment

I — Inspiration

Customers could arrive without knowing what happened next

In store visits, I repeatedly saw customers park in a curbside space, wait, then walk to the service desk to switch to in-store pickup. That switch could send associates moving an order from one end of the store to the other. Our goals were to reduce missed pickups and fulfillment changes, improve the customer experience, and shorten fulfillment times.

I talked with customers, associates, and store managers. Customers described waiting, sometimes calling the store or opening the app, without receiving a signal that their arrival had been acknowledged or their order was on its way.

A Wi-Fi gate could signal arrival to the store if a customer had the app, was logged in, and connected to Wi-Fi. Even that small cohort received no confirmation back from the store. The system could detect an arrival without resolving the customer’s uncertainty.

Customers expected pickup in under five minutes, yet about 30% called to change their pickup method. The opportunity was to make the wait more predictable and reduce the disruption those changes created.

D — Design Process

Separate arrival access from customer feedback

The running strategy was to market the mobile app and encourage more customers to log in. That could help operations, but it left the feedback gap open. Weak parking-lot cell and Wi-Fi signals could prevent check-in, and customers sometimes crossed the arrival gate before running errands nearby.

I proposed two complementary changes: pickup emails would let customers share an ETA and check in without downloading the app; app notifications would confirm check-in, provide a recovery path when it failed, and announce that an order was coming out.

E — Engagement

Win support for a pilot beyond the app

Making pickup easier through email could reduce the incentive to download the app. I built a proposal that weighed that concern against customers’ uncertainty and the operational cost of changing pickup methods.

I won support for a limited regional pilot of the email improvements and app notifications. That let the team evaluate the customer and store benefits before committing to a broader change.

A — Action

Make arrival easier, then close the feedback loop

The existing curbside confirmation email advertised other pickup options, making it unclear which method was selected and encouraging a switch that inconvenienced customers and associates. I focused the updated email on the selected pickup method, collection instructions, ETA choices, help, and Spanish-language access.

Closing the loop for app users

Alongside the email improvements, we added app notifications that gave customers an expectation or a recovery path after check-in.

Three states answer three different questions

Arrival acknowledged
The store knows you are here. The notification gives a ten-minute expectation.
Check-in failed
The arrival was not confirmed. Call the store to recover.
Order coming out
The order is on its way. Wait at the selected pickup location.

S — Success

Clearer expectations in the store pilot

≈90%
Reported that pickup arrived when expected
3.8 min
Average door-to-door time with an ETA
<10%
Called to change pickup method, versus about 30% before the pilot

Reported results from a 60-day pilot in 50 stores; retrospective figures have not been independently revalidated.

During the pilot, average door-to-door time was 3.8 minutes for customers who shared an ETA, compared with 4.5 minutes for those who didn’t.

My takeaway: an arrival signal helps the store prepare, and a confirmation helps the customer wait. Both sides need feedback when the process changes.
